desc:
Count the contiguous subarrays of nums (of any length, at least 1) whose largest element minus smallest element is at most limit. Subarrays at different positions are counted separately even if their values are equal.

nums = [5, 1, 3, 4, 2, 9], limit = 3
length 1: 6 subarrays      length 2: [1,3] [3,4] [4,2] -> 3
length 3: [1,3,4] [3,4,2] -> 2      length 4: [1,3,4,2] -> 1
result = 12
constraints: The answer is at most n(n+1)/2, which fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: Testing all O(n<sup>2</sup>) subarrays with max and min recomputed each time is too slow. First think about how to count the valid subarrays that end at a fixed position.
If [l, r] is valid then [l+1, r] is valid too. So for each right end r the valid left ends form a contiguous range l..r, and the smallest such l never decreases as r grows.
Slide a window with two monotonic deques (max and min of the window). After shrinking from the left until the spread is within the limit, add r - l + 1 to the answer.
editorial: Fix the right end r and let l(r) be the smallest left end for which nums[l..r] is valid. Subarrays only get more constrained when they grow, so every start from l(r) up to r works, which gives r - l(r) + 1 valid subarrays ending at r. Also l(r) is non-decreasing in r.

Maintain the window [l, r] with a decreasing deque (maximum) and an increasing deque (minimum) of indices. When a new element makes the spread exceed the limit, advance l and discard deque fronts below l. Add r - l + 1 to the total at each step. Linear time because each index enters and leaves each deque at most once.
